title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
gist: Explainer arguing surveillance (personalized) pricing, which uses personal data to infer each customer's maximum willingness to pay, is growing as data brokers, e-commerce and machine learning make it easy, with the FTC counting at least 250 companies using it in 2025. Examples include Instacart, Target, Orbitz, ZipRecruiter and Tinder; the author urges disclosure, a preference for dynamic over surveillance pricing, and consumer price discipline.

themes.theme: Definition and economics of surveillance pricing

insights.claim: Surveillance pricing is an algorithmic practice that charges different individuals different prices for the same goods by using personal data to infer the highest price each customer will pay, unlike dynamic pricing which responds to market supply, demand, inventory and competitor prices.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a regulatory-risk pricing practice from more defensible surge pricing.

insights.claim: The FTC said in 2025 that at least 250 companies used surveillance pricing.

insights.claim: Surveillance pricing is likely to become more common because of its lucrativeness, growing availability of user data from data brokers, IoT and web tracking, advances in machine learning, and the shift to e-commerce.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Data brokers and pricing-AI vendors stand to benefit, while retailers face reputational and legal risk.

insights.claim: Consumer Reports found in 2025 that Instacart's personalized price variations could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year for a typical household of four; Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Shows backlash can force platforms to abandon personalized pricing, affecting revenue optimization.

insights.claim: Target's app was accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV when they were inside a Target store, and Orbitz was found in 2012 to feature more expensive hotels to macOS users.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Illustrates how retailers already use device and location data to steer prices.

insights.claim: Tinder agreed to pay $60.5 million to settle a class action alleging it charged older users more for subscriptions, while denying it used demographic data for pricing.

insights.claim: The American Economic Liberties Project argues surveillance pricing relies on biased algorithms, citing higher rideshare prices to predominantly non-white neighborhoods and test-prep pricing over $1,000 higher in zip codes with large Asian populations.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Discrimination evidence raises the likelihood of legislation banning or restricting the practice.

insights.claim: Some critics argue for legislation banning surveillance pricing, while others contend bans could hurt consumers because personalized pricing can also show lower prices.

insights.claim: Companies could disclose when personalized pricing is used, as Uber does with surge pricing, and prioritize dynamic pricing over surveillance pricing to maximize revenue while reducing the risk of biased pricing.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Disclosure-plus-dynamic-pricing is a likely compliance path for platforms facing scrutiny.

insights.claim: Surveillance pricing incentivizes ever more detailed consumer data collection, which data brokers share with third parties including law enforcement for unrelated purposes.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Links pricing practices to broader privacy regulation risk for data brokers.
